Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-04-22
- Start: 15:00 PDT
- Duration: ~1h2m
- Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Kai Patel (Redwood CSM); Priya Nair, Mike Thompson, Emily Zhou, Carlos Rivera (Arcadia)
- Recording: (available)

Summary:
Quick triage on latency variance observed in last pilot run. Focus: TTFT spikes, streaming jitter, sequence length sensitivity, and kernel selection effects. Goal: produce prioritized experiments and next steps for dedicated node bench.

Topics covered:
- Recent pilot numbers: TTFT median vs 95th, microburst behaviour
- Streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs (token flush / chunk sizing)
- Seq length distribution and fallback quantization impacts
- Kernel matrix tests (amx vs fused attention) and impact on cold start
- Security/ops questions: VPC egress, KMS for keys, SOC2 scope for logs

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Sofia Martinez: hey everyone, thanks for joining. uh we'll try to keep this tight, we've got an hour, um, thanks Arcadia team for pulling traces. can you confirm Priya?
[00:00:12] Priya Nair: yeah confirmed, we uploaded a sampled 24h trace and a 48h heavier trace, it's in the s3 path in the invite notes, i think carlos also added a network dump.
[00:00:22] Carlos Rivera: yep put the peering config and a small tcpdump, i mean it's pretty coarse but should help.
[00:00:29] Jordan Lee: great, so quick agenda - i'll show the kernel sweep we ran yesterday on the pilot image, then we'll look at the traces for microbursts and first-token variability.
[00:00:37] Mike Thompson: quick note - we saw some runs where first token took like 480ms and others 120ms, so big variance, not sure if it's batch sizing or infra.
[00:00:45] Jordan Lee: right, that aligns with our initial run: median TTFT ~130ms but p95 jumps to 430ms during microbursts. we suspect a combo of k-v cache cold starts and intermittent OS scheduling.
[00:00:58] Emily Zhou: when you say k-v cache, do you mean the prefix cache or the key-value cache for attention? sometimes the naming in the reports gets swapped.
[00:01:06] Jordan Lee: yeah, sorry, the kv cache for attention, the per-request kv warmup. i also use "prefix cache" to mean our prefix hit cache, so.. nomenclature confusion there.
[00:01:15] Sofia Martinez: totally, also expect some mislabels in the auto-transcribed logs we pulled.

[00:02:10] Jordan Lee: i'm sharing my screen — the kernel matrix: we tested 6 kernels across sequence length buckets (16/64/256) and both streaming and non-streaming modes. results were noisy but consistent: amx-fused attention gave best median for long seqs but higher cold-start. the fused kernel seems to allocate larger scratch buffers which hit memory pressure and cause eviction cascades.
[00:02:39] Priya Nair: can you repeat the last bit about scratch buffers? we saw OOMs in one run but blamed k8s pod limits.
[00:02:46] Jordan Lee: sure. the fused kernel needs bigger temporary buffers at compile time, so on small node configs it can push GPU memory right up and then other inflight evictions cause the runtime to stall — which shows up as spike in TTFT. Kubernetes pod limits can mask this but the underlying memory churn is still there.
[00:03:03] Mike Thompson: interesting. so is the mitigation increasing reserved GPU mem or switching kernels per seq length?
[00:03:09] Jordan Lee: both are options. we recommend a kernel routing policy: short sequences use the lightweight amx-simple kernel, long sequences go to fused. that reduces spikes without overcommitting memory.
[00:03:21] Carlos Rivera: how do you route at runtime? is that a separate process or built-in?
[00:03:26] Jordan Lee: it's runtime policy in the serving layer — we evaluate sequence len at request start and pick kernel. it's fast, <1ms decision. but there is also the fallback where if a kernel runs out of memory we fallback to a compatible variant.

[00:04:40] Sofia Martinez: we also saw streaming behavior — chunk size and flush cadence matter. some of Arcadia's client streams send tiny chunks which increases overall per-token overhead.
[00:04:49] Priya Nair: yeah, our frontend does 1-2 token flushes on typing. is there recommended chunk size?
[00:04:55] Jordan Lee: typically 8-16 token chunks is a good sweet spot. very small chunks add RPC overhead and reduce batching efficiency. for typing UX you can emulate optimistic UI and buffer 8 tokens then flush, or use progressive partials.
[00:05:08] Emily Zhou: but we care about first-token latency for user experience when the prompt is short — we can't wait for 8 tokens.
[00:05:14] Jordan Lee: understood — for TTFT we have fastpath profiling: pre-warm kv entries for common prefixes and aggressive microbatching with burst slots on dedicated nodes. that keeps TTFT low while still using chunking for longer responses.

[00:06:25] Mike Thompson: curious about dedicated vs hosted - we are evaluating dedicated GPUs for predictability. what's the delta in latency variance?
[00:06:32] Sofia Martinez: with Dedicated reserved nodes you remove multi-tenant noise and can tune kernel memory more aggressively. p95 can drop significantly — e.g., in our benchmarks p95 reduced from ~430ms to ~210ms in similar workloads, but there is tradeoff with cost.
[00:06:47] Priya Nair: and how does that interact with KMS? we need keys in our KMS, not yours.
[00:06:52] Sofia Martinez: we support customer-managed KMS/HSM for Private and Dedicated — Redwood's control plane can be configured to use your KMS via IAM roles and key wrapping. we'll share integration notes.
[00:06:59] Carlos Rivera: do you log tokens? audit logs are a concern.
[00:07:05] Kai Patel: by default we keep limited telemetry for latency and cost; sensitive data can be redacted and logs can be sent to customer's log sink. SOC2 scope and logging policies are in the security packet Sofia will send.

[00:08:40] Jordan Lee: back to performance: we plotted TTFT vs request rate and microburst frequency. when bursts coincide with model cache misses, you see exponential degradation because cache fill operations are serialized. we think Arcadia has some patterns where short/high-frequency requests cause cache churn.
[00:08:56] Priya Nair: can you point at where in our traces that happens? we gave you the 00:00-06:00 and 18:00-22:00 windows where we observed it.
[00:09:04] Jordan Lee: yes in the 18:00 window the median is fine but p95 spikes correlate with a tail of tiny-reqs. i highlighted some trace IDs in the sheet. those map to short sequences with low prefix reuse.
[00:09:17] Mike Thompson: is it worth changing client behavior to batch client-side? we can change UX but it's heavy lift.
[00:09:23] Sofia Martinez: small client-side batching is lighter — 50-200ms buffer before sending is one option, optimistic echoing is another. we should evaluate UX tradeoffs.

[00:10:45] Jordan Lee: experiment plan suggestion: 1) kernel routing by seq len, 2) microbatch slots for bursts on dedicated nodes, 3) streaming chunk size to 8 tokens for test group, 4) run microburst bench with our script to reproduce.
[00:10:58] Priya Nair: sound good. for the microburst bench, what infra do we need?
[00:11:05] Jordan Lee: we can run on your existing pilot nodes or spin dedicated capacity in Redwood Dedicated trial for a week. for fidelity, dedicated nodes are better. we can also synthetic generate the same pattern as your traces.
[00:11:17] Emily Zhou: budget wise we prefer to try on pilot nodes first, then escalate if we see improvements.

[00:12:30] Mike Thompson: question on quantization - we tried int8 and saw a small latency benefit but weird output regressions sometimes. any suggestions?
[00:12:37] Jordan Lee: quantization can change logits; we recommend model-specific evals and can suggest per-layer quant profiles. also for TTFT you might not see large token-level latency wins unless memory bandwidth is the bottleneck. quant helps throughput more.
[00:12:53] Priya Nair: okay we'll keep quant in staging until evals pass.

[00:14:00] Sofia Martinez: a few ops notes — Carlos, you mentioned network egress: we need baseline egress numbers to factor into routing and cost. also sonic spikes we saw might be due to VPC NAT gateway scaling.
[00:14:10] Carlos Rivera: i'll pull NAT logs and share baseline.

[00:14:50] Jordan Lee: i'm going to describe the kernel matrix csv naming: kernel,seq_bucket,mode,median_ms,p95_ms,notes. i'll upload to the pilot folder. samples show fused-amx best at 256 but p95 worse on 16/64.
[00:15:04] Priya Nair: can you annotate run ids so we can map to traces?
[00:15:10] Jordan Lee: yes will include run ids.

[00:18:30] Sofia Martinez: security quick check — we support SAML SSO, RBAC, and audit logs. for SOC2 we can provide the compliance pack and a summary of how logs are retained.
[00:18:41] Emily Zhou: fine, we'll review. any red flags?
[00:18:44] Kai Patel: no red flags, just standard mapping items. Sofia will share the packet.

[00:21:00] Jordan Lee: noting an oddity: some autoscaling events in your cluster overlapped with pilot runs — when nodes spin up CPU/GPU scheduling can cause brief stalls. if possible, freeze autoscale during bench.
[00:21:11] Carlos Rivera: we can schedule bench windows, yes.

[00:25:00] Sofia Martinez: recap and decisions: run kernel routing experiment, run streaming chunking test, run microburst bench on pilot nodes first, prioritize dedicated bench if variance persists. security docs to be shared. next sync after we have kernel csv and production traces.

[00:25:20] Emily Zhou: timeline — can we see results next week?
[00:25:24] Jordan Lee: we'll push initial csv and a short writeup by 2026-04-29.
[00:25:30] Priya Nair: we'll get traces to you by 2026-04-25.

[00:30:00] Sofia Martinez: alright thanks everyone, we'll follow up in thread with links.
[00:30:06] Mike Thompson: thanks, bye.
[00:30:09] Priya Nair: thanks bye.
